title: Acute Headache Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for acute nontraumatic headache in adults presenting to the emergency department, covering life-threatening secondary causes and common primary headache disorders.
source_description: ACEP Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Evaluation and Management of Adult Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Acute Headache. Godwin SA, Cherkas DS, Panagos PD, Shih RD, Byyny R, Wolf SJ. Ann Emerg Med 2019;74(4):e41-e74.

diagnoses.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)
red_flags: Sudden onset to maximal intensity within seconds to minutes
Age 40 years or older with new thunderclap headache
recommended_tests: Non-contrast CT head (within 6 hours of onset)
Lumbar puncture (if CT negative and clinical suspicion remains)

diagnoses.name: Bacterial Meningitis
recommended_tests: Non-contrast CT head (before LP if focal deficits or altered mental status)

diagnoses.name: Cervical Artery Dissection
key_features: History of minor trauma or neck manipulation
red_flags: Neck pain following trauma or chiropractic manipulation
recommended_tests: CT angiography of head and neck

diagnoses.name: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis (CVT)
key_features: Headache worse with recumbency or Valsalva
red_flags: Headache in peripartum or postpartum period
Oral contraceptive use with progressive headache

diagnoses.name: Intracranial Mass Lesion (Tumor)
key_features: Worse in morning or with Valsalva
red_flags: New headache in patient with known malignancy

diagnoses.name: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis)
red_flags: Scalp tenderness with temporal artery abnormality

diagnoses.name: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
key_features: Severe unilateral eye pain and headache
Blurred vision with halos around lights
Red eye with fixed mid-dilated pupil

diagnoses.name: Hypertensive Emergency
key_features: Severe headache with markedly elevated blood pressure
red_flags: Systolic BP greater than 180 or diastolic greater than 120 with end-organ damage

diagnoses.name: Migraine
key_features: Aura (visual, sensory, or speech disturbance) in some patients
recommended_tests: Neuroimaging only if red flags present

diagnoses.name: Tension-Type Headache
key_features: Not aggravated by routine physical activity

diagnoses.name: Cluster Headache
key_features: Severe unilateral periorbital or temporal pain
Autonomic features: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, ptosis
Attacks lasting 15 to 180 minutes, occurring in clusters
recommended_tests: MRI brain to exclude secondary causes on first presentation

also_consider.name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)
also_consider.rationale: Progressive headache with papilledema and visual obscurations; more common in obese women of childbearing age; check opening pressure on LP

also_consider.name: Pituitary Apoplexy
also_consider.rationale: Sudden severe headache with visual field deficits and ophthalmoplegia from hemorrhage or infarction of pituitary adenoma; neurosurgical emergency

also_consider.name: Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS)
also_consider.rationale: Recurrent thunderclap headaches over days to weeks; often triggered by vasoactive drugs, exertion, or postpartum state; angiography shows segmental vasoconstriction

also_consider.name: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
also_consider.rationale: Headache with nausea, dizziness, and confusion; ask about cohabitants with similar symptoms; check carboxyhemoglobin level

also_consider.name: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES)
also_consider.rationale: Headache with seizures, visual changes, and altered mental status in setting of hypertension, eclampsia, or immunosuppressive therapy

also_consider.name: Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension (CSF Leak)
also_consider.rationale: Orthostatic headache dramatically worse upright and relieved supine; may follow LP or epidural; MRI shows pachymeningeal enhancement

also_consider.name: Viral Encephalitis
also_consider.rationale: Headache with fever, altered mental status, and behavioral changes; HSV encephalitis requires urgent acyclovir; temporal lobe involvement on MRI

also_consider.name: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
also_consider.rationale: Headache with proptosis, chemosis, and ophthalmoplegia; often secondary to facial or sinus infection; urgent CT venography

also_consider.name: Acute Sinusitis
also_consider.rationale: Facial pain and pressure worsened with bending forward; nasal congestion and purulent discharge; usually does not present as primary headache complaint to ED

also_consider.name: Pre-eclampsia / Eclampsia
also_consider.rationale: Headache with hypertension, proteinuria, and edema in pregnant or postpartum woman; seizures indicate eclampsia; obstetric emergency

also_consider.name: Third Ventricle Colloid Cyst
also_consider.rationale: Intermittent severe positional headache from transient obstruction of foramen of Monro; can cause sudden death from acute hydrocephalus

also_consider.name: Cerebral Abscess
also_consider.rationale: Headache with fever and focal neurological deficits; risk factors include endocarditis, sinusitis, dental infection, or immunocompromise

also_consider.name: Medication Overuse Headache
also_consider.rationale: Chronic daily headache in patient using analgesics more than 10 to 15 days per month; rebound pattern; treatment requires withdrawal of offending agent

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. The ACEP clinical policy emphasizes that ruling out subarachnoid hemorrhage alone is insufficient -- clinicians must consider other dangerous secondary causes such as cervical dissection, cerebral venous thrombosis, and encephalitis. Use the Ottawa SAH Rule and SNOOP mnemonic to guide risk stratification. Consider atypical presentations in elderly, immunocompromised, pregnant/postpartum, and anticoagulated patients. A normal non-contrast CT does not exclude all secondary causes.
